Subject: What's actually in DC tap water
Preview: Chlorine, chloramine, and why your city chose one over the other.

---

Words I like;
"If you wouldn't put it in your coffee, why would you put it in your body?"
Your DC tap water is treated. That's good. It keeps you safe from bacteria and pathogens that plagued cities 100 years ago. But what they add to make it safe doesn't just disappear when it hits your glass.
Most municipal systems use chlorine or chloramine. Chlorine is older, cheaper, breaks down faster (which is why some cities switched). Chloramine is chlorine bonded to ammonia. It's more stable, lasts longer in the pipes, and doesn't create the same disinfection byproducts chlorine does.
DC Water uses chloramine. So does most of the metro area. That's why your tap smells faintly like a pool some mornings, or why filling a fish tank without treatment can kill everything in it within hours.
Chloramine doesn't boil off. It doesn't evaporate. A basic pitcher won't touch it. It takes catalytic carbon, contact time, and flow control to remove it properly. If you already own one of our city water systems, that's exactly what's happening every time you turn on the tap. You made a smart call.
If you're still on straight municipal, hit reply and I'll send you a free water assessment.
As promised, value in under a minute.

## Executive Summary

The competitive landscape remains stable this week with no major messaging shifts detected. Mermaid Water continues aggressive promotional bundling (4+ concurrent offers including $200 water heater discounts and free installation on Kinetico systems), maintaining their position as our primary local threat in Northern Virginia. EcoWater is leaning heavily into their "Water Pro" consultant branding and third-party certification messaging, positioning themselves as the science-backed national alternative. Hampton Roads Water Services is emphasizing their lifetime warranty and "Made in USA" manufacturing as key differentiators in the Tidewater/Richmond corridor.
